strengths: Addresses a practically important setting: unlearning using only the pretrained model and forgetting data. The target-versus-other-logit sensitivity objective is simple and directly optimizable.

Reports strong class and subclass results. MU-Mis achieves average accuracy gaps of 0.07 percentage points on full-class CIFAR-100 and 0.20 on CIFAR-20-Sea, competitive with methods using retained data. Runtime savings are substantial in several comparisons.

The evaluation includes multiple datasets and architectures, sequential deletion, loss-term ablations, sensitivity-regularized training, and two membership attacks. Pseudocode, implementation details, hyperparameter tables, and a code link provide useful reproducibility support.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is insufficiently established. Section 3.2 drops the dependence of probabilities and the training trajectory on the perturbed training sample without bounding the resulting error. Appendix D does not establish that cross-sample terms are small, particularly after summation over the dataset. Moreover, sensitivity to an infinitesimal input perturbation is not equivalent to influence under sample deletion. These arguments do not justify identifying the optimized sensitivity gap with the contribution that unlearning must remove.

The mathematical presentation contains substantive errors. Section 3.2 reverses the cross-entropy logit-gradient sign: it should be p minus the one-hot label. Equation A7 omits the softmax-Jacobian contribution to the input loss Hessian. For locally affine logits, its expression predicts zero curvature even though cross-entropy generally has nonzero input curvature. These errors weaken the claimed theoretical grounding.

The broad utility-preservation and superiority claims exceed the evidence. In Table A8, MU-Mis has retained accuracy 70.48% versus 100% for retraining and test accuracy 57.37% versus 84.45%; its average gap is 19.85 versus 0.84 for RUM. Table A7 also shows smaller utility gaps for SCAR on CIFAR-10 and several remaining-data-free baselines on SVHN. The appendix acknowledges limitations, but the abstract and main-text claims remain substantially too broad.

The practical stopping and tuning protocol is not convincingly validated without retained-data access. Thresholds vary from 0.68 to 3.00 across individual tasks and reach 10 in sequential deletion, whereas the sensitivity study covers only 0.7–1.0 on one task. Important experiments additionally use a reweighted objective with kappa=80 and manually changing schedules. The paper needs to explain how these choices are selected without retained-data or retraining feedback and demonstrate that they transfer to new deletion requests.

Privacy conclusions are stronger than the attack evidence supports. A low fraction of forgotten samples classified as members does not establish indistinguishability from retraining. The additional SCRUB-LiRA evaluation is useful, but attack calibration and operating characteristics are insufficiently documented; its random-subset score is 52.66% versus 49.68% for retraining. There is also an unexplained discrepancy between Tables A7 and A11: MIA-Entropy for the same CIFAR-10 deletion setting is 33.04 versus 83.34.

Some implementation details remain ambiguous despite the extensive appendix. Random-subset experiments fix the irrelevant class to class 1, without explaining how samples whose true label is 1 satisfy the required different-class condition. Table A13 reports different L2 and Frobenius results without clarifying their aggregation, although these norms coincide for a vectorized single-logit input gradient.
